prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and time-reversal-invariant topological insulators, and for the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B038 as my single-part preference, and the full first-round exchange has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. This is a discovery in the sense I think the committee should care about most: Kane and Mele identified a new organising principle (the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant band insulators, with symmetry-protected helical edge states), and Molenkamp's group showed within two years that nature realises it, with a conductance signature that could have falsified the idea. It has since been confirmed in independent material families (HgTe, InAs/GaSb, Bi2Se3 and related compounds by ARPES) and has changed how band structures are classified and how materials are searched for. The result is roughly two decades old, so maturity is not in question, and it is the only leading entry where a theory-plus-experiment pairing maps onto exactly three names without forcing an exclusion. I also want to be clear about my own reasoning. In round 1 I partly cited broad cross-member ranking as a reason to move from inflation; I now regard that as the weaker argument and do not rest on it. The reason I stay is the scientific one: a clean new concept, a decisive falsifiable test, and long independent confirmation. I am persuaded by Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce that I overstated the overlap of the lattice clock with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and I move B046 up to my first alternative. I do not move it to first place, because I still weigh a new organising concept above the best realisation of an existing measurement idea, but I would not regard a Katori and Ye prize as a mistake.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and I do not think it can be argued away. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe quantum-well realisation that Molenkamp's experiment tested, and the three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane and Mele; Moore and Balents; Hsieh and Hasan) lies outside the three credited names. A prize to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp tells a defensible but incomplete story, and the committee should accept that openly rather than describe the chain as clean. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions and topological phases will also be cited against it, and the practical payoff (dissipationless edge transport, spintronics) has not materialised. The chair's question about whether the citation can avoid the gap is the crux. I think it can only be done by scoping the citation to the Kane-Mele prediction and the first observation in HgTe, and by stating explicitly that the prize does not cover the HgTe proposal or three-dimensional topological insulators. If a majority finds that scoping unfair to the people left out, B046 is the cleaner alternative, and I would rather support it than force a contested attribution.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B038 because the Z2 classification is a concept-level result confirmed across several material families, and he accepts that the credit chain is incomplete and that the citation needs careful wording, including the fact that the Kane-Mele graphene model itself is not what was observed.
responses.response: I agree with the weighing of concept over instrument and with your caution about graphene: the spin-orbit gap there is too small, so the honest story is prediction in the Kane-Mele framework and observation in HgTe, which is how the citation is now worded. Where I would press you is on how far the committee should go to defend the trio. Your reply to Olsson suggests that the Kane-Mele credit is the conceptual origin and the HgTe proposal is an application. I think that understates it, because without the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal the experiment would not have been designed as it was. I would not pretend the gap is small. I would say plainly in the public statement that the prize is for the Z2 prediction and the first observation of the quantum spin Hall state, and that it does not adjudicate the HgTe proposal or the three-dimensional work. We should concede that cost rather than hide it.

responses.point: Kroll argues that lattice clocks are the only entry pairing a single sharply defined idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms with Lamb-Dicke confinement) with an unambiguous quantitative payoff, reproduced at the 1e-18 level in several laboratories, and that neither the 2005 nor the 2012 prize contained that idea.
responses.response: This moved me on one point and not on another. In round 1 I described the lattice clock as a refinement of a line already honoured in 2005 and 2012. Your argument, which Pearce and Lindroth also make, is right that neither the comb nor single-ion control contains the magic-wavelength idea that removes the light shift while keeping many atoms, so the overlap is real but limited and I withdraw the stronger version of my objection. I also agree that the prize should not wait for the redefinition of the second, which is another body's decision. What I keep is a difference in prize philosophy: where two results are both mature and verified, I would give more weight to a new organising concept that changed what physicists look for than to the best realisation of a measurement idea, and I recognise that you weigh this the other way. That is why B046 is my first alternative and not my preference.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the 2016 prize concerned topological phase transitions and Hall conductance and does not make the clock's rival redundant, and she states that the Katori and Ye division into concept and realisation is an honest description of two separable contributions.
responses.response: On the credit split for B046 I find your reasoning persuasive: Katori's proposal and first strontium clock, and Ye's record accuracy and many-body clock work, are separable and the citation can say so. That lowers my concern about a two-name prize and is part of why I now rank B046 first among my alternatives. On B038 I would add that you and I read the 2016 overlap the same way, as a distinct symmetry-protected classification, but I think the committee should not treat that as settled just because three of us agree. The risk is that the public message looks like a second topological prize, and the citation should lead with time-reversal symmetry, spin-orbit coupling and the absence of an external field to make the distinction visible.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B042 because the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction was followed by the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, which have been reproduced across several moire platforms, and he replied to my round-1 point that independent confirmation across material families gives the field stability.
responses.response: I accept your correction that the moire field is not resting on a single laboratory, and the extension to twisted transition-metal dichalcogenide systems is a genuine sign of robustness; I withdraw the suggestion that reproducibility is the issue. My remaining concern is narrower. The prediction is elegant and the observation secure, but the credited set has Cao, Fatemi and the earlier continuum-model authors outside it, and the pairing mechanism, while it need not be in the citation, leaves open how the committee would describe the achievement in a sentence. For topological insulators the sentence writes itself. I regard B042 as a strong candidate for a later year rather than this one, and I do not rank it among my alternatives for 2026.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B046 first on the grounds that it has the cleanest two-name attribution on the list and the strongest form of verification, direct clock-to-clock comparison across independent laboratories, and he says he would rather give Kane, Mele and Molenkamp a prize than reopen the clock case if the clock is found unconvincing.
responses.response: I accept the verification point: independent clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level are the strongest form of confirmation an experiment can have, and in that respect the clock is more directly checked than any other entry. I also agree that you and I are not far apart on what the fallback should be. The place I differ is on how much weight a clean attribution chain should carry against a conceptual contribution. A two-name split is tidy, but tidiness is not the same as importance, and I would not accept the argument that B038 is ruled out by its attribution gap if the citation is scoped to the prediction and first observation. I would, however, ask the committee to be consistent: if the standard is a clean attribution, B046 meets it better, and I would not block it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a B038 citation scoped to the Kane-Mele prediction and the first HgTe observation, or will regard the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang as unfair enough to defeat the entry.

Whether B038 should be understood as covering only the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, or whether the three-dimensional topological insulator work must be acknowledged, which would bring in names outside the credited set.
How much distance the committee sees between the 2016 prize on topological phases and a time-reversal-invariant Z2 prize; I think it is distinct, but this is a judgement and not a settled fact.

How much weight to give a new organising concept relative to a verified instrument-level invention when both are mature; I recognise that this is a prize-philosophy difference and not an objective ranking, and that it is the main reason I stay apart from the B046 camp.
I am recalling priority and timing details for the HgTe proposal and the strontium lattice clock history from memory and have not verified them from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B038 or for my alternatives B046 and B032. I work in theoretical high-energy physics and cosmology, which makes me closer to B032 than to the condensed-matter and atomic-physics entries, and I hold no known connection to any credited name for those entries. My documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) do not involve any shortlisted candidate. I note Eriksson's work in two-dimensional materials at Uppsala and Kroll's Boulder proximity as disclosed by them, and I do not think either affects my own position.
